title: How much richness (photos, detail) to put on a screen
plain_english: Solen's current rule is one flat number: about a third of every browse card should be photo. This research shows real competitor apps (Fresha, Airbnb, Urban Company, CVS Health) don't use one flat percentage everywhere, they size the photo zone to what the screen is asking the user to do. A profile page gets a bigger photo block up top, a browse list keeps the existing third, and a checkout or time-picker step goes almost photo-free and still feels polished, not broken. It also confirms a ceiling on how many distinct things a screen shows above the fold: four to seven grouped chunks, never a wall of items.
the_rule: Size the imagery zone to the task: hero/profile pages get one photo zone at roughly 35-45% of the first screen, browse/list cards keep the existing ~1/3 floor, and checkout/booking-step screens (cart, slot picker, payment) drop to near-zero imagery on purpose. Above the fold, cap distinct grouped items at 4 to 7, biased to 4-5 on mobile.
tier_summary: Miller 1956 chunk-limit (T1, strongest tier) plus real shipped-app corroboration (Fresha, Airbnb, CVS Health, Urban Company); the imagery-zone bands themselves are single-example observations (T3/CONV), not proven causal, pending a Solen taste-lab test before they get locked in as hard numbers.
top_sources: Miller 1956, working memory (7±2 chunks)
Fresha and Treatwell live salon pages (real fetches)
Airbnb, CVS Health, Urban Company, Square Go app screens (Mobbin observations)
before_state: Solen's FLOORS LAW says browse cards should be about 1/3 photo (owner-approved). That number gets applied as if it were the right number everywhere, there is no separate guidance for a profile/hero page versus a checkout or booking step.
after_state: The 1/3 floor stays exactly as-is for browse cards. New guidance is added for two other zones: hero/profile pages should run a bigger photo block (about 35-45% of the first screen), and checkout/booking-step screens should intentionally go near-photo-free, that is correct, not a gap to fill. Above-the-fold item count is capped at 4 to 7 grouped chunks, and browse/discovery screens can lean richer while booking-commit steps (Zeit, Bezahlen) should stay sparse.
visual_demo_desc: Wrong: the same photo-heavy treatment used everywhere, a big decorative photo block bolted onto the time-picker/payment step next to the slot grid. Right: three panels showing the zone-sized approach, a salon profile page with one ~40% hero photo, a browse grid with ~1/3 photo per card, and a booking time-picker step that is flat, text and pill-first, with zero photos.
one_line_why: Richness isn't a flat percentage you paint over every screen, it's a zone sized to what the screen is asking the user to do.

title: Picking the right container: list, grid, carousel, table, or bento
plain_english: Right now the choice of "list vs grid vs carousel vs bento box" for any screen with multiple items (salons, services, bookings, dashboard KPIs) is made by habit, not by a rule. This addition gives a simple test: are the items all the same kind of thing or different kinds, and does the user need to compare them or just browse a preview. That test picks the right container every time, and explains why forcing same-kind items (like plain salon listings) into a trendy bento grid reads weaker and messier, while bento only works for a handful of genuinely different things, like a dashboard mixing a chart, a number, and a list.
the_rule: List is the default for same-kind, uncapped, comparable sets (search results, services, booking history). Add a list+map split-view only when location/distance actually matters to the decision. Grid is for a small bounded set (roughly 4-8 items) that must be fully scannable at once. Carousel is only for a small preview of a bigger set, with a "See all" escape hatch, never the only place the full set lives. Table becomes a wrapped chip-grid or an explicit Table/Chart toggle on mobile; real tables stay desktop-only. Bento is only for a small fixed set (roughly 2-6 cells) where every cell is a genuinely different kind of thing, never the same kind of item just resized bigger or smaller.
tier_summary: Baymard controlled usability testing (T2) for the map split-view numbers, real competitor-app observations (T3, mostly re-verified this cycle) for the container examples, plus PSYCHOLOGY.md law 11 (T1) for the carousel-hides-options rule
top_sources: Baymard Institute, accommodation search split-view study
Fresha and Uber real-app observations (re-verified, one correction made to the Uber attribution)
PSYCHOLOGY.md law 11, Comparability beats trimming
before_state: Not covered yet. Solen has no written rule for which container to use for a group of items; LOCKFILE only classifies the content's shape (manuscript/column/modular/hierarchical), not the concrete container to build.
after_state: A clear decision test: count the items, check if they're the same kind of thing or different kinds, and check if the task is compare vs browse-preview vs read-a-fixed-set. That test names the container (list, split-view, grid, carousel, table-or-chip-grid, or bento) before any mockup gets built, and flags that Solen's distance-ranked salon search may be a candidate for a list+map split-view, pending an owner decision, since it currently may sit in the underperforming list-only bucket Baymard measured.
visual_demo_desc: Wrong: a row of same-kind salon result cards (name, photo, rating, distance) forced into an uneven bento grid with big and small tiles, looking cluttered and hard to scan in order. Right: the same salons shown as a clean vertical list, and separately, a small handful of genuinely different dashboard tiles (a chart, a number, a shortcut) shown as a proper bento grid.
one_line_why: Match the box to the content: same-kind things line up in a list, only genuinely different things earn a bento grid.

title: Hero height should match the page's job, not one fixed number
plain_english: When building a brand-new page, the top "hero" block (photo, search bar, or icon) should be sized based on what the page is for, not a single memorized percentage. A search-and-browse page (Solen's home or a salon list) wants a shorter hero so people get to searching fast; an empty-state screen wants a smaller centered cluster; only a rare full-bleed brand intro screen should go big. Using the same hero size everywhere makes some pages feel top-heavy and others feel thin.
the_rule: Pick hero height from the page's job, not one flat number: search/browse marketplace pages get roughly 30-50% of the first screen (a wide, still-soft range); empty-state or single-action screens get roughly 20-30% height as a centered cluster (icon, heading, and button grouped together, not pinned to the top); a full-bleed brand or onboarding hero can run up to 80-85%, but only as a rare outer limit, never a default. This replaces Solen's current habit of using "about 40%" as a flat hero size on every new page.
tier_summary: T3 directional evidence (live re-checks of Fresha and Treatwell, plus app screen reads via Mobbin), backed by one solid CONV-tier fact, the 8pt spacing grid convention. The review pass downgraded the original CONV claim because none of the hero percentages were ever pixel-measured, only read from page summaries.
top_sources: Live re-check of Fresha and Treatwell homepages
Urban Company, Depop, and TIDE app screens (Mobbin)
8pt/8px spacing grid convention (Material Design, IBM Carbon)
before_state: Solen's own notes currently treat "hero about 40% of the screen" as a general rule for any new page. That number actually came from tuning one specific screen (EmptyStateDiscovery), not from a rule meant to cover every page type.
after_state: New pages get sized by job: search/browse pages target roughly 30-50% hero height, empty-state screens target a smaller centered 20-30% cluster, and a full-bleed hero is kept as a rare upper bound, not a default. The exact numbers are still soft, flagged for a follow-up test (build one real Solen page at 25%, 35%, and 55% hero height and have the owner squint-test which reads right) before locking a final number.
visual_demo_desc: Wrong: a search/browse page (e.g. category hub) with a flat 40% hero regardless of job, crowding out the search bar and pushing content far down. Right: the same page's hero shortened to sit in the 30-50% band so the search bar and first content row appear higher on screen, with an empty-state screen shown alongside using a smaller centered 20-30% icon-heading-CTA cluster instead of a top-anchored one.
one_line_why: A hero's height should answer "what is this page for," never "what did the last page use."

title: A recipe for empty states (no bookings yet, no search results, first-run screens)
plain_english: Right now Solen has one polished empty-state screen, the discovery rail people see when they have no favorites or looks saved yet, but there is no general recipe for building the next empty screen (a search with zero results, a new empty list) without a fresh design decision every time. This adds that recipe so future empty screens stay consistent instead of each one being invented from scratch.
the_rule: Every empty state has 4 parts, always in this order: a visual sized to 15 to 40 percent of the block's height (small icon for a secondary empty state, bigger illustration or, better, real data for a main one), a headline of 3 to 6 words naming what's missing, one grey subline saying what will appear (never an apology), and exactly one button (solid ink for a main empty state, a plain text link for a small nested one). One question is still open for the owner: what color the "reset filters" button should be on a zero-search-results screen. Three real options are on the table (solid ink, neutral outline, or a plain text link), not decided yet.
tier_summary: Solen's own shipped, owner-approved EmptyStateDiscovery component (strongest evidence) plus a re-checked Mobbin scouting pass across Fresha, Peerspace, CRED and Freenow (real live apps, observed pattern, not a scientific study)
top_sources: Solen's EmptyStateDiscovery component (shipped, owner-confirmed 2026-06-11)
Mobbin screen captures: Fresha, Peerspace, CRED, Freenow
Eleken / LogRocket design-literature consensus on empty-state anatomy
before_state: Solen has one real empty-state component (EmptyStateDiscovery, real salon data instead of a drawing) used on 3 profile pages, but no written rule for any other empty state. Each new one (search-zero-results, onboarding, a new empty list) would need a fresh design call from scratch, and the zero-results button color has never been decided.
after_state: A written 4-part recipe (visual, headline, subline, one button) that any new empty screen gets built against automatically, so it starts consistent with the rest of Solen instead of waiting on a design review. The one real gap left is a named, three-option question for the owner about the zero-results button color, not a guess.
visual_demo_desc: Wrong: a bloated empty state with a big full-bleed illustration, an apologetic paragraph of text, and two competing buttons fighting for attention. Right: a small icon or real-data module at about a quarter of the screen height, a short headline like "Noch keine Buchungen", one grey line under it, and a single solid ink button.
one_line_why: An empty screen isn't nothing, it's four small decisions doing one job: show what's missing and give the person exactly one way forward.

title: How layouts should collapse on smaller screens
plain_english: Right now Solen has one grid rule (2 columns, then 3, then 4 as the screen gets wider) with no real logic behind why. Looking at how Fresha, Airbnb, Booking.com and Turo actually behave, the right collapse behavior depends on what kind of content it is: photo/card grids (like salon search results) should hold their column count almost all the way down and only drop to one column on a phone, while dense list-and-sidebar content (like a filter panel) should stack much earlier, already at tablet width. Maps and filter chips have their own rules too. Getting this right means new pages don't need to be redesigned later when someone views them on a different screen size.
the_rule: Four defaults for any new responsive component: (1) card/photo grids hold their column count from desktop down to tablet, dropping to 1 column only on phone (under 768px); dense list-plus-sidebar content stacks a full breakpoint earlier, already at tablet (768px). (2) A map or detail panel next to content is never resized smaller, it is either shown full-size or swapped for a single open/close button. (3) Filter and chip rows never wrap to a second line, they scroll sideways instead. (4) A multi-field control (like a search bar) either merges into one summary pill or stacks as separate full rows, chosen once per product and kept consistent, not decided per screen size.
tier_summary: T2, directly re-rendered and reconfirmed live on Fresha, Airbnb, Booking.com and Turo (not secondhand reports)
top_sources: Fresha search results (live render, 375/768/1440)
Airbnb search results (live render, 375/768/1440)
Booking.com and Turo search results (live render, contrasting cases)
before_state: Solen's design lockfile states one bare grid recipe (2 columns to 3 to 4 columns as screens widen, with a note for when the map is open) but with no explanation of why, and no rule at all for how filter rows, search bars, or map panels should behave as the screen shrinks. Nothing today distinguishes "photo grid" content from "dense list" content.
after_state: New responsive components get built right the first time using four named defaults, instead of guessing per component. It also surfaces a real question worth showing the owner: Solen's current grid adds a third column at tablet width, but Fresha and Airbnb (the two apps Solen is modeled on) both hold at 2 columns through tablet when their map is open, which matches Solen's own map-open rule. What's untested is what Solen's grid does when the map is closed, that's the one open decision to bring to the owner via a side-by-side comparison.
visual_demo_desc: Wrong: a search-results grid at tablet width (768px) that has already jumped to 3 cramped, oddly-narrow columns just because it's "not phone-sized" (no rationale, doesn't match Fresha/Airbnb). Right: the same grid holding 2 wide, comfortable columns at tablet width, matching Fresha and Airbnb, dropping to a single column only once it hits phone width.
one_line_why: Reflow by what the content is, a photo grid and a data table don't deserve the same breakpoint.

title: Imagery amount stays a parked question, not a rule
plain_english: This one is not actually a new design rule. It is a note confirming a real question is still waiting on you: how much photo content should search results, PDP bodies, and dashboards carry. That gate (G6) was declined back on 2026-07-15, and this pass confirms nothing has changed since. It matters because photos clearly help bookings once they exist (Airbnb saw a real occupancy lift from professional photos), but nobody has set a target amount of photo coverage for Solen's own surfaces yet.
the_rule: No number to apply yet. The only figure on file is a competitor snapshot (Uber: 34% illustration, 28% photo, 38% chrome across 116 images), which is a reference point, not a validated target. A real answer needs either a fresh study or a small test on the search results grid comparing 2-3 photo-to-text ratios.
tier_summary: Airbnb occupancy study (T2, one strong peer-reviewed paper) plus a Baymard vendor benchmark (T3); the Uber imagery mix is T3, an internal competitor measurement, not a proven optimum
top_sources: Management Science (Airbnb photo occupancy study)
Baymard Institute usability benchmarking
LOCKFILE.md Uber imagery inventory (V3-D330)
before_state: Solen has 6 category hero photos specified (PHOTO_STRATEGY.md) and a locked Uber-style imagery layout pattern in LOCKFILE section 11, but no rule for how much photo content the search results grid, PDP body, or dashboard should carry beyond those heroes. This gap has sat declined since 2026-07-15.
after_state: Nothing changes today. A parking note gets added to the research file spelling out exactly what a yes from you would unlock (a density target for those surfaces) and how it would get tested (2-3 photo-to-text ratio versions of the search results grid, shown to you as real pages, asking which feels complete versus cluttered versus bare). It stays parked until you say go.
one_line_why: Photos sell the chair, but nobody has measured how many photos is enough, so guessing a number here would be inventing data, not applying it.

title: Keep the stepper and CTA in the same spot across every booking step
plain_english: When a customer moves through a multi-step flow like Services to Staff to Time, the feeling of "this flows together" does not come from fancy animation between screens. It comes from keeping the step indicator and the bottom button in the exact same spot on every screen, and only changing their fill, label, or price on that fixed spot. Screen changes should just be a quick directional slide, and if a sheet or picker is opened, its result should land back in the exact row that opened it, not somewhere new.
the_rule: Pin at most two anchors per flow (the step indicator and the bottom CTA/price bar) to an identical on-screen position on every step. Show progress only as a fill, label, or color change on those fixed anchors, never as a new element appearing somewhere else. Step transitions stay directional slides at or under about 300ms (Solen's existing V3-D464 booking slide already meets this). A sub-flow's result (sheet, date/time picker) must render back into the exact row that opened it.
tier_summary: Baymard Institute usability research (T2) plus Airbnb's own engineering writeup (T2, verified quote) on why per-element choreography, corroborated by Solen's own already-shipped V3-D464 timing
top_sources: Baymard Institute checkout flow UX research
Cal Stephens, Airbnb Tech Blog (Motion engineering at scale)
Foundey Stepper UI Best Practices (downgraded to CONV, uncredentialed blog)
before_state: Solen's booking flow already uses a slide+fade transition (V3-D464, glide curve) between steps, which happens to already sit under the 300ms ceiling, but there is no explicit rule that the stepper and CTA must stay pinned to the identical position across all three steps, and no explicit assertion that a sub-flow's result (like the DateTimePicker) must render back into the exact row that opened it.
after_state: The booking flow gets a named, explicit rule: the step indicator and bottom CTA/price bar stay in the same spot on every screen (Services, Staff, Zeit), only their fill, label, or value change to show progress. The DateTimePicker's committed result renders into the same row that opened it, by design, not by accident. Shared-element photo morphs (like Airbnb's flagship transitions) stay rare, reserved for the existing card-to-PDP moment only, unless the owner runs the taste-lab probe and decides booking earns a second one.
visual_demo_desc: Wrong: three booking screens (Services, Staff, Zeit) each with the stepper and CTA button in a different vertical position or size, so the layout jumps between steps. Right: the same three screens with the stepper and CTA pinned to the identical spot on every screen, only the stepper's fill dot and the CTA's label/price changing.
one_line_why: Continuity is a fixed address, not a moving animation, the feeling of flow comes from what stays put, not what flies in.

title: How to add a new design token correctly
plain_english: Solen has a rule for its neutral gray colors (a fixed 12-step ramp) but no rule for adding anything else: a new accent color, a new spacing gap, a new corner radius. This addition gives one procedure for all three: figure out if the new value fits an existing slot or is genuinely new, generate it with a formula instead of eyeballing a hex code, and name it so the name itself tells you what it is. It matters because a hand-picked token today is exactly the kind of hardcoded hex or one-off spacing value that breaks consistency later and slips past review.
the_rule: Before minting any new token: (1) classify it as fitting an existing ramp or table (extend, the default) or truly new (open, needs an owner yes logged in TASTE_LOG first); (2) derive the value by formula, not by eye, placed into the existing ramp position (color follows Radix's 12-step map, steps 1-2 backgrounds through 11-12 text; spacing follows near-doubling from the 4px base, never a picked number; radius matches Material's role bands, which Solen's own 12/16/20/28/pill table already lines up with); (3) name it with four fixed questions, value kind, UI role, variant, state, for example s-color-background-loyalty-platinum, never by hue or vibe; (4) a component may never point straight at a raw value, it must go through the semantic layer first; (5) run any new token through the existing solen-drift-check gate like every other token.
tier_summary: Radix Colors' 12-step ramp and Tailwind v4's OKLCH shift, re-checked live (CONV), plus WCAG contrast math (T1). Material Design 3's tone and shape scales are well-established general knowledge (CONV) but not freshly re-fetched. One claim was caught and cut during verification: Uber Base's claimed CI gate on token merges could not be confirmed, so the enforcement idea now stands only on Solen's own existing drift-check gate.
top_sources: Radix Colors (radix-ui.com/colors)
Material Design 3 token and shape system (m3.material.io)
Tailwind CSS v4 OKLCH theme layer
before_state: Solen's domain 19 covers only the neutrals ramp: a generator exists for gray steps, but there is no naming grammar and no rule stopping a component from pointing straight at a raw value for anything outside neutrals (a new accent color, a new spacing gap, a new radius).
after_state: Any new token, color, spacing, or radius, goes through the same three checks: is it really new or does it fit an existing slot, is the value derived by formula rather than picked, and does its name alone answer what kind of value, what role, which variant, which state. New tokens route through the same solen-drift-check gate Solen already runs, so a hand-picked value gets caught before it ships.
one_line_why: A token is not really designed until you can say which formula placed it and which four words name it, not which vibe picked it.

title: Card density should shrink while scrolling, grow while deciding, and the "no price on cards" rule is a Solen choice, not a copy of Fresha
plain_english: How much information sits on a card should change depending on what the customer is doing. When they're scanning lots of salons or scrolling the Inspo feed, cards should be light (few fields, no price, no button). When they land on one salon's page to actually decide, the layout should relax with more padding and one clear top to bottom flow. The research also caught a mistake in the earlier draft: it claimed Solen's "no price on search cards" rule copies Fresha's structure, but a live recheck of the real Fresha search page shows Fresha actually puts prices and a booking preview on every card. So Solen's no-price card is our own deliberate choice, not something inherited from Fresha, and that should be named honestly rather than implied.
the_rule: Discovery/Inspo feed: 2-column masonry, roughly 8-12px gutter, no caption overlays on tiles, about 3 rows visible per mobile screen. PDP: generous padding, about 90-100px per content row with a hairline divider between rows, no photo per row. Search results: density band not yet safe to lock (the Fresha anchor was wrong), but the direction holds: scanning surfaces stay light, the decide surface (PDP) gets more breathing room. Flagged, not a locked rule yet, pending an owner call on the search card.
tier_summary: T1 live re-check of the real Fresha search page (which overturned the original claim) plus T2 Mobbin corroboration from Square Go PDP, ClassPass, Pinterest, and Lemon8
top_sources: Fresha search page (live re-rendered, corrected)
Square Go salon PDP (Mobbin)
ClassPass search list (Mobbin)
before_state: Solen's current search cards show no price and no per-card button, and this was implied to be "matching Fresha's structure." Discovery feed and PDP density had no researched default at all, just eyeballing.
after_state: Discovery feed and PDP now have a researched density band to build against (masonry gutter, rows-per-fold, row height). But the search-card claim is corrected, not locked: Solen's no-price card is flagged as our own deliberate deviation from Fresha, and the file proposes a side-by-side owner review (current no-price card vs an accurate Fresha-style priced card) before anything here gets written into the locked design system.
visual_demo_desc: Wrong: label Solen's current thin, no-price search card as "matches Fresha's structure" (the false claim from the first draft). Right: show Fresha's actual live search card, which carries a photo, name, distance, category, and up to three priced services with a "view more services" link, side by side with Solen's card correctly labeled "our own choice, diverges from Fresha on purpose."
one_line_why: Density is a decision that should shrink while a customer is scanning and grow once they're deciding, and copying a competitor's structure by accident is worse than diverging from it on purpose.

title: A computable "is this screen balanced" number, advisory only
plain_english: This adds a way to compute a number for whether a screen's visual weight (bigger and higher-contrast elements count more) sits off-center, instead of relying purely on eyeballing it. The number is only a flag for a human to glance at during the existing squint-test review, never an automatic pass or fail. It matters for a booking app because it catches genuinely lopsided screens without punishing Solen's deliberate restrained, mostly-white-and-black look, which would look "underweighted" if judged by a formula tuned on flashier competitor apps.
the_rule: Compute each element's weight as its size times its local contrast, find the weighted center point of the whole screen, and only flag it if that center point drifts more than about 15% off the true middle on either axis. Below 15%, say nothing. This is a proposed default, not a locked number, and it never blocks a build or joins any automatic drift gate.
tier_summary: NN/g's qualitative balance definition (T2, verified verbatim) plus real-app convergence across 9 unrelated apps' empty states (CONV); the academic centroid formula itself (Lok/Feiner/Ngai 2004) turned out to be a loose inspiration only, not a validated match, and its claimed "5 student" study was found to not exist
top_sources: Nielsen Norman Group, Balance in UX Design
Lok, Feiner & Ngai, ACM IUI 2004 (WeightMap model)
Figma Check Designs (Oct 2025), non-blocking precedent
before_state: Solen judges screen balance only by eye, through the manual squint-test step inside the solen-taste-diagnosis skill. There is no computed number behind that judgment today.
after_state: The squint-test pass gets an optional computed number alongside it (a percent offset per axis) that flags only gross imbalance, calibrated against Solen's own screens rather than flashier competitor apps, and never turns into an automatic gate.
one_line_why: A number can flag a lopsided screen for a human to check, but it should never get to vote on its own.

title: Blue accent audit: split "clickable blue" from "meaningful color"
plain_english: This adds a fix to how Solen's automatic blue-color checker works. Right now it risks flagging things like the green success check, the yellow star, or the orange surcharge tag as "too much color" just because they are not black or grey, even though those colors carry real meaning and are not decorative blue. The fix tells the checker to count blue separately from meaningful status colors, so it stops giving false alarms on correct design and only clamps down on blue actually used as decoration.
the_rule: Split the accent-color check into two counts: clickable blue (cap at 1 distinct blue hue per screen, the existing sparse-blue rule) versus semantic status colors (green success, red error, yellow star, red save-heart, orange surcharge), which are exempt and never count against the blue-sparsity limit because they carry meaning, not decoration. The existing numeric ceilings (3 blue instances on content screens, 1 on forms) are NOT changed by this, that number stays open for a future owner decision, not applied here.
tier_summary: Treisman and Gelade 1980 (T1, why a rare color pops out) plus WCAG 1.4.11 (T1, contrast law) anchor the principle; the competitor evidence (Uber, Airbnb, Fresha, Doctolib) is real but thin, and a verification pass caught two fully fabricated screen citations (American Airlines, HotelTonight) and one invented quote (Airbnb "one or two moments"), all removed before this went final.
top_sources: Treisman and Gelade 1980, Feature Integration Theory (Cognitive Psychology 12:1)
WCAG 2.1 Success Criterion 1.4.11 (Non-text Contrast)
Uber design system teardown, superdesign.dev/blog/uber-design-system
before_state: Solen's LOCKFILE already bans a blue-filled primary CTA and a blue price, and a blue-sparsity metric spec exists with an unsourced roughly-3-instance ceiling. But the metric that counts "how many distinct accent colors are on screen" does not separate clickable blue from Solen's own semantic status colors (success green, error red, star yellow, save-heart red, surcharge orange), so a correctly-used semantic color could get wrongly flagged as an invented, off-brand hue.
after_state: The accent-color metric gets a scoping fix: only blue counts toward the "1 clickable accent hue" ceiling. The five semantic status colors are explicitly exempted since they mean something specific and are not decoration. The two hard-fail rules Solen already has (no blue CTA, no blue price) are reconfirmed by real counter-examples found on IKEA (blue-filled CTA) and, more shakily, a claimed American Airlines blue price that turned out to be a fabricated citation and was removed. The actual numeric ceiling (3 vs 2 blue instances) stays parked for the owner to decide later, nothing here silently tightens it.
one_line_why: Blue reads as "click me" only while it stays rare, so an automated color check must count blue and meaning-carrying colors separately, or it will punish the app for using green, yellow, and orange correctly.

title: Catch near-miss misalignment with a script, not an eye
plain_english: Sometimes two things that should line up (like all card edges in a row) are off by just 1 to 4 pixels, close enough that it looks like a mistake, not a deliberate design choice. Right now the only way to catch this is a human noticing it. This adds a script that measures every relevant edge and spacing value on a page and flags the near-misses automatically, so a booking card row or a form doesn't ship looking subtly crooked.
the_rule: Two elements only count as "aligned" if their edges match exactly (0px apart). A gap of 1 to 4 pixels is flagged as a mistake to fix. Anything bigger than 4px is assumed to be an intentional design choice (like a staggered card) and left alone. Separately, every spacing or padding value should be a multiple of 4 (or a multiple of 5 or 10 once it's above 100px), matching Solen's existing grid rule.
tier_summary: Grounded in Solen's own already-locked rules (RATIONALE.md, T2) plus real-world corroboration that this exact kind of check is normal, shipped tooling: Figma's own AI Consistency Checker and the Galen Framework's alignment-testing pattern (CONV, both directly confirmed).
top_sources: RATIONALE.md (Solen's own alignment/grid rules)
Figma AI UI Consistency Checker (figma.com)
Galen Framework spec language (galenframework.com)
before_state: No automated check exists. Misalignment (like a card row where one edge is a few pixels off) is only caught if a person happens to notice it during manual review.
after_state: An advisory script can scan a rendered page, measure every edge and spacing value, and produce a punch list of near-miss misalignments and off-grid spacing before the page ships. It never blocks work automatically, it just feeds the pre-delivery check.
visual_demo_desc: Wrong: a row of three booking cards where the middle card's left edge sits 3px off from the other two, a subtle but visible crookedness. Right: the same three cards with all left edges landing on the exact same pixel, clean and steady.
one_line_why: If it's not on the same coordinate, it's not actually aligned, it just looks like it might be.

title: A mandatory 6-point self-check before any UI turn ends
plain_english: Right now, checking a design for hierarchy, contrast, spacing and so on is advice that can be skipped when in a hurry. This adds a gate: after any UI change, the turn cannot end until 6 specific checks are each reported as pass or flagged with a fix. It works the same way a mandatory pre-flight checklist works in surgery or aviation, an optional checklist gets skipped under pressure, a mandatory one does not.
the_rule: Before any UI-touching turn ends, report all 6 axes (squint test, hierarchy count, type-size ceiling, grouping, contrast ratio, density) each as PASS or FLAG-with-fix. All 6 must clear, not a majority, or the turn is blocked.
tier_summary: Wharton et al. 1994 cognitive walkthrough (T1) plus WHO Surgical Safety Checklist trial, Haynes et al. NEJM 2009 (T2, verified: complications 11.0% to 7.0%, mortality 1.5% to 0.8%, 8 hospitals, 7,688 patients)
top_sources: Wharton, Rieman, Lewis, Polson (1994), The Cognitive Walkthrough Method
Haynes et al., NEJM 2009, WHO Surgical Safety Checklist trial
Deputy onboarding review + GitLab/Graphite merge gates (Mobbin-confirmed, each check its own truthful row)
before_state: Solen has the solen-taste-diagnosis skill and the six-axis self-walk as a documented method, but nothing forces it to run, an agent can eyeball a change and call it done without ever touching the checklist.
after_state: A Stop hook blocks the turn from ending on any UI edit until all 6 checks are explicitly reported, pass or flagged with a fix. Not yet built, this session flagged it needs the owner's go-ahead first, and self-testing before it gets wired in, per the build-test-then-integrate rule.
one_line_why: A checklist only changes behavior when skipping it is impossible, not when skipping it is merely discouraged.

title: Two structured ways to pin down "that looks off"
plain_english: Right now when you say a screen feels "too heavy" or "too busy" without naming why, or you dispute one specific value like a shadow or radius, there is no repeatable process to settle it, so the same vague complaint can resurface later. This adds two small structured sessions: one shows three real screens and asks which two feel alike and how the third differs, repeated until no new idea comes up, to name the actual thing being reacted to. The other narrows in on one disputed number (corner roundness, blue intensity, shadow depth, motion speed) by repeatedly asking "closer to this or that" until the answer stops moving. Both get written down once so the same argument never has to happen twice.
the_rule: A vague complaint said twice with no named cause triggers a "which two of these three screens feel alike, how does the third differ" session, repeated until two rounds in a row produce no new idea (typically 6-10 rounds). A disputed specific number (radius, shadow, blue intensity, motion speed) triggers a "closer to A or B" narrowing session, stopped after 3 direction reversals, taking the average of those last 3 as the answer, using accept-as-settled bands of about plus or minus 2px for radius, plus or minus 20ms for motion timing, plus or minus 0.05 for opacity or saturation. Either result gets written into the taste log once, dated, so it is not re-argued later.
tier_summary: Kelly 1955 and the Fransella, Bell and Bannister repertory grid method (verified academic technique) for the "which two are alike" session, plus Cornsweet 1962 psychophysics staircase method (verified) for the number-narrowing session. The specific stopping counts (2 rounds, 3 reversals) are reasonable defaults chosen for this use, not numbers proven in the literature.
top_sources: Kelly, G.A. (1955), The Psychology of Personal Constructs
Fransella, Bell and Bannister, A Manual for Repertory Grid Technique
Cornsweet, T.N. (1962), The Staircase-Method in Psychophysics
before_state: No repeatable process exists to convert a vague, repeated taste complaint ("too heavy", "too busy") or a disputed specific value (a radius, a shadow, a blue tone) into a settled, written decision. The same complaint can get re-argued from scratch each time it comes up.
after_state: A vague repeated complaint gets a short "which two screens feel alike" session that names the real issue as a clear before/after pair of words. A disputed number gets narrowed down through repeated "closer to A or B" choices to a specific value within a small tolerance. Both outcomes get written into the taste log once, dated, so the decision sticks and does not get relitigated.
one_line_why: Name the taste dispute once, in the owner's own words, and it never has to be argued twice.

title: Tap-target size and slip-adjacency sweep
plain_english: This adds a check for two separate things: is a button big enough to tap, and is a dangerous button (cancel, delete) sitting too close to a safe one so a user could hit the wrong one by mistake. Right now Solen has no check at all for the second problem, and one design doc even cites the wrong accessibility standard for the first. For a booking app where Cancel and Reschedule sit next to each other constantly, this catches the exact mistake that makes someone cancel an appointment by accident.
the_rule: Two checks. (1) Target size: any tappable element under 24x24px is a hard fail (the legal accessibility minimum), under 44x44px is a soft warning (Solen's own stricter house floor). (2) Slip adjacency: if a destructive button (cancel or delete) sits within 24px of a safe or commit button, flag it, unless the two are told apart by color, by weight (solid button versus plain text link), or by structure (a second confirm screen in between).
tier_summary: W3C WCAG 2.5.8/2.5.5 spec text (T1, directly verified) plus an 8-app Mobbin real-world scout, Fresha, CVS, Lime, Shift (T2)
top_sources: W3C WCAG 2.2, Understanding Target Size Minimum and Enhanced
DubBot, Designing Destructive Buttons (2025)
Mobbin real-app captures: Fresha, CVS Health, Shift, Lime
before_state: No slip-adjacency check exists anywhere in Solen. Target size is only checked informally, and SOURCE.md line 1032 wrongly credits the 44px hit-area rule to WCAG 2.1 (that standard does not contain this rule at all, it was added in WCAG 2.2). Solen's CTA system is ink-only, so it also has no color set aside for destructive actions.
after_state: A sweep automatically flags any tap target under 24px (hard fail) or under 44px (soft warning), plus a new check that catches a cancel or delete button sitting too close to a safe button unless it is set apart by color, weight, or an extra confirm step. The wrong WCAG citation gets corrected to WCAG 2.2. Left open for the owner to decide: whether Solen should add a dedicated destructive red color, since today it has no color-based way to mark danger, so new destructive controls must rely on a downgraded control style or an extra confirmation step instead.
visual_demo_desc: Wrong: Shift's Reschedule and Cancel shown as two identical buttons, same size, same color, same weight, side by side with only a small gap, so a user could tap the wrong one without noticing. Right: CVS Health's pair, Reschedule as a solid filled button and Cancel as an outline-only button with a clear vertical gap, so the eye tells them apart before the finger does.
one_line_why: A button that is easy to tap is not the same as a button that is safe to tap next to its more dangerous neighbor.

title: Catch the same UI role rendered two different ways
plain_english: Right now Solen's drift checker only looks at one file at a time, so it can catch a stray hardcoded color or a wrong duration in that file. But if a card on the homepage uses one corner radius and the exact same kind of card on another page uses a different one, both pass, because each one is "legal" on its own. This addition adds a second check that compares the same role (card corner radius, selected-pill color, price formatting) across every place it's used, and flags it the moment two places disagree.
the_rule: Register a role (like "card-radius" or "tabpill-selected-fill") with its LOCKFILE-locked value. Scan every place that role appears. If a spot doesn't match the locked value, block the commit (hard stop). If there's no locked value yet, just log the mismatch so it can be decided later (soft flag), not blocked.
tier_summary: Nielsen 1994 usability heuristic (T1, verified) plus a live-measured Fresha component check (T2, independently re-confirmed)
before_state: The existing drift checker only catches violations inside one file at a time (a hardcoded hex, a wrong duration). A component that uses a legal style at one call site and a different legal style at another call site passes every existing check, because nothing compares across files. This is exactly what happened with the TabPill selected-state regression that was only caught by a manual screen check, not automatically.
after_state: A new check groups by role across the whole codebase, not per file. If every instance of "card radius" or "selected pill color" matches the locked value, it passes silently. If even one instance differs from the locked value, the commit is blocked automatically, the same way a hardcoded hex color gets blocked today.
visual_demo_desc: Wrong: two salon cards from different pages sit side by side, one with sharp-ish 8px corners and one with rounder 16px corners, same component, different look. Right: the same two cards side by side both showing identical 16px rounded corners, so they read as one consistent design system.
one_line_why: If the same kind of thing looks different in two places, people read it as a bug even if neither one broke a rule by itself.
top_sources: Nielsen Norman Group, consistency and standards heuristic
Live getComputedStyle audit of fresha.com (Card_--radius-m)
Solen RATIONALE.md, Twin-control rule

title: Spacing rhythm: gaps inside a group must read smaller than gaps between groups
plain_english: When items are grouped on a screen, like rows inside one settings section, the space between items in the same group has to look clearly tighter than the space before the next group starts. If those two gaps are close in size, or the "between" gap isn't bigger, the eye can't tell where one group ends and the next begins, so the screen reads as one long confusing list instead of organized sections. This adds an automated check that scans a rendered Solen page and flags any spot where that ordering is broken.
the_rule: The gap between items inside the same group must always be smaller than the gap to the next group. This gets checked automatically on every render, and it is the strict, must-fix part of the check. A softer, unproven idea says neighboring spacing values should differ by at least a 1.25x ratio to look visually distinct, but that number is only a guess borrowed from typography, not a measured rule, so it stays advisory and never blocks anything.
tier_summary: Strong: Wertheimer 1923 and Kubovy and Wagemans 1995, both top-tier perception science, backed up by 8 real apps checked on Mobbin (Base, Instagram, Uber, and 5 others) all following the same pattern with zero exceptions. Weak: the 1.25x ratio number is an unproven guess, and its supposed source (an NN/g article) was checked directly and found to not contain that ladder of numbers at all, so that citation was struck as fabricated during verification.
top_sources: Wertheimer 1923, Gestalt Proximity
Kubovy and Wagemans 1995, Psychological Science
Mobbin real-app scout: Base, Instagram, Uber, Careem, Grab and others
before_state: Solen's rules already set spacing tiers (32 for sections, 12 for cards, 16 for groups), but nothing automatically confirms a given screen actually follows the "tighter inside a group, looser between groups" rule. A spacing mistake could ship unnoticed.
after_state: A read-only automated check now scans any rendered page and flags any group where the internal spacing is not clearly smaller than the spacing before the next group, catching a real Gestalt-proximity violation before it ships. It never auto-fixes and never touches a locked spacing value, it only flags.
visual_demo_desc: Wrong: a settings list where the gap between rows inside one section is about the same size as the gap before the next section's header, so the whole list looks like one continuous unbroken block. Right: the same list where rows inside a section sit close together and a clearly larger gap appears right before the next section header, so the sections read as distinct groups at a glance.
one_line_why: Space is a language: let the gap inside a group whisper and the gap between groups shout, or the eye can't tell where one group ends and the next begins.

title: Catch German (and French/Italian) text before it clips a button or pill
plain_english: German, French, and Italian words are often much longer than the English ones Solen is designed around, especially in short labels like buttons, pills, and tabs where German can run 200 to 300 percent longer. This addition is a concrete way to test every screen in all four languages and automatically flag any text that gets clipped, overlaps something else, or breaks out of its box, instead of finding out only after a user in Zurich sees a cut-off word. It was proven necessary by finding this exact bug live on Fresha and Booking.com today, both of which clip real German text in production.
the_rule: Test every screen at 375/768/1280px in all four languages (de/en/fr/it) and auto-flag four failure types: text clipped inside its own box, a box that grows too tall, a box that bleeds past its container with no scrollbar, or two elements that now overlap. For short labels (under 10 English characters, i.e. most buttons and pills), allow up to 200 percent growth before flagging; longer text gets a smaller allowance (down to 130 percent for long paragraphs).
tier_summary: WCAG 1.4.4/1.4.10 (T1, the clipping/overlap rule itself) plus IBM/W3C's text-expansion table (T3) and two independently reproduced live failures on Fresha and Booking.com's own German mobile sites (T2)
top_sources: W3C WCAG 2.1 (SC 1.4.4 Resize Text, SC 1.4.10 Reflow)
IBM/W3C Internationalization text-expansion table
Live capture: Fresha.com and Booking.com German mobile, this session
before_state: Solen ships de/en/fr/it translations but has no automated check for whether the longer German/French/Italian text actually fits inside buttons, pills, tabs, and other fixed-width elements. This is essentially unchecked today. RATIONALE.md itself contains a transcription error in the expansion-percentage numbers it currently cites (roughly half of the real values).
after_state: A reusable audit (built on the existing site-tester crawl tool, no new vendor) renders every route in all four languages at three breakpoints and produces a pass/fail list: clipped text and broken layouts are blocking, unusually long wraps are flagged for review. Short, high-frequency UI strings like button and pill labels get the strictest check since they are the highest-risk category.
visual_demo_desc: Wrong: a German button or filter pill with its label ellipsis-clipped mid-word ("Aktueller Sta...") or a checkbox label cut off with no ellipsis at the edge of a fixed 3-column row, exactly like the live Fresha and Booking.com screenshots. Right: the same element either sized wider to fit the full German word, or given a short-verb label so it never needs to grow.
one_line_why: If it only fits in English, it does not actually fit.

title: Show severity as a word, not a number, worst-first
plain_english: Right now the design-finding severity score (D10) is a computed number behind BLOCKING/HIGH/MINOR/COSMETIC labels. This adds the display rule: never show the raw number to a human, only the word, always sorted worst first, and if a finding also needs a second tag (like "gate breach" or "mechanized"), that stays a separate small tag next to it, never squashed into one label. Grouped lists also get a count next to each tier name, like "BLOCKING (3)", so a shrinking count between review rounds is visible at a glance instead of something you have to recount by hand.
the_rule: Print only the tier label (never the 0-4 score), sort worst-first, keep a second field (like source) as its own adjacent tag never fused with severity, and show a count on each tier heading (e.g. "BLOCKING (3)").
tier_summary: Nielsen severity math (T1, live-reconfirmed) plus the display convention observed on real tools, strongest on Jira and ClickUp (both native fields), Airtable and Asana template-strong, GitHub Projects and Miro downgraded to weak/anecdotal after verification
top_sources: Nielsen Norman Group: How to Rate the Severity of Usability Problems
Nielsen Norman Group: Heuristic Evaluation Theory (35% single-evaluator figure)
Mobbin captures of Jira and ClickUp priority displays
before_state: D10 already computes BLOCKING/HIGH/MINOR/COSMETIC from the severity math, but nothing in the spec says how it should actually be displayed to a reader (as a number, a label, sorted how, combined with what).
after_state: The same four labels stay exactly as they are (no new tiers, no new math). What changes is purely how punch lists and SUGGESTIONS.md render them: word only, worst first, source shown as its own separate tag, and a count on each group heading.
visual_demo_desc: Wrong: a punch-list panel showing a raw number like "Severity: 3.2", items in random order, and a fused label like "HIGH-gate_breach" mashed together with no count on the group header. Right: the same panel showing clean group headers "BLOCKING (3)", "HIGH (2)", "MINOR (5)" in that order, each item showing just its tier word plus a small separate tag like "gate_breach" beside it, no numbers anywhere.
one_line_why: A number makes the reader do math in their head; a word plus a shrinking count tells them the story at a glance.

title: Navigation: breadcrumbs, tab bars, and the single back button
plain_english: The real question behind this research was what actually makes navigation feel easy or hard in a booking app. The answer is not the number of taps to get somewhere, it is whether the user always knows where they are (the label or title predicts what comes next) and whether controls like "back" always work the same way everywhere. A scan of 13 real booking and marketplace apps (Fresha, Airbnb, Klook, Booksy, and others) found that none of them show a breadcrumb trail in the actual search-to-booking path, only in help or support sections. They all keep a visible 3 to 5 icon tab bar instead of hiding navigation behind a hamburger menu, and every one uses a single, consistent back button.
the_rule: Keep a visible tab bar of 3 to 5 destinations, never hide it behind a hamburger menu. Skip breadcrumbs on the actual booking path, even on a page that is 2+ levels deep where Solen's own rule technically allows one, since 0 of 13 competitor apps show a breadcrumb there. Keep the single global back button as is. Tap or click count alone is not what to optimize: a well-labeled 25-step path beats a poorly-labeled 3-step one, so clear labels matter more than fewer taps.
tier_summary: NN/g's own studies (179-participant hamburger-menu test, breadcrumb guidelines) plus a 13-app competitor scan (Fresha, Airbnb, Klook, Booksy, and 9 others)
top_sources: Nielsen Norman Group (hamburger-menu study, breadcrumb guidelines)
Joshua Porter's three-click study, already flagged as myth in Solen's own folklore table
13-app competitor scan (Fresha, Airbnb, Klook, Treatwell, and others)
before_state: Solen's breadcrumb rule (show one starting at 2+ page levels deep) and single-global-back rule already existed, but were justified mainly by brand analogy and button-placement logic (Fitts's Law), not by cited research or a look at what real competitor apps actually do on their booking path.
after_state: The same two rules stay locked exactly as written (nothing changes today), but are now backed by NN/g's studies and a 13-app scan showing zero competitors use a breadcrumb in their transactional flow. It also adds a caution: never collapse the tab bar into a hamburger menu as destinations grow, and adds a note for later that Solen's 2+ level breadcrumb threshold might eventually be worth moving to match NN/g's 3+ floor (logged as an open question, not decided now).
visual_demo_desc: Wrong: a salon booking flow screen cluttered with a breadcrumb trail ("Home > Coiffeur > Zurich > Salon X > Buchen") stacked above the page title, competing with the header for attention. Right: the same screen with just a clear page title acting as the landmark and a single back chevron top-left, no breadcrumb, matching what Fresha, Airbnb, and Klook all do on their real booking screens.
one_line_why: Depth does not cost you, losing your bearings does: skip the breadcrumb, keep the compass.

title: Filters should show the count, and never dead-end
plain_english: When someone is narrowing down search results with filters, they should always see what they're about to get before they commit, and they should never land on a blank "no results" screen with nothing to do. This matters for Solen because Angebote search already lets people stack filters, so a zero-result dead end (wrong combination of category, date, price) is a real risk that quietly loses the user right at the moment they were closest to booking.
the_rule: Filter sheets should restate the live result count on the commit button itself (for example "21 Ergebnisse anzeigen" instead of a bare "Anwenden"), and a zero or low-result screen needs one tappable recovery action, either relax the tightest filter or show a fallback set of results, never just apologetic text with nothing to click.
tier_summary:
Hearst 2006 faceted-search research (T2) plus real-app convergence on live-count commit buttons across 7+ booking apps (Zocdoc, eBay, Glassdoor); Baymard Institute no-results research (T3) plus convergence on structural recovery across 12+ apps (ClassPass, HelloFresh, Too Good To Go)</tier_summary>
<parameter name="top_sources">["Marti Hearst 2006, Design Recommendations for Hierarchical Faceted Search Interfaces", "Baymard Institute, 5 Proven UX Strategies For No Results Pages", "Zocdoc / ClassPass / HelloFresh live app captures (Mobbin)"]
before_state: Solen's Angebote search already has single-select filters that AND-combine on the backend (locked product decision), but nothing yet governs what the filter sheet's commit button says or what happens on a zero-result combination. This mechanic is not covered yet.
after_state: The Angebote filter sheet's commit button restates the live count ("21 Ergebnisse anzeigen") instead of a bare "Anwenden", and a zero or sparse-result screen gets one clear recovery action (a button that relaxes the tightest filter, or a relabeled fallback set of results) instead of a plain "keine Ergebnisse" message with no way forward.
visual_demo_desc: Wrong: filter sheet with a plain black "Anwenden" button, and a zero-result screen showing only grey text "keine Ergebnisse" with nothing to tap. Right: the same filter sheet with the button reading "21 Ergebnisse anzeigen", and the zero-result screen showing an icon, a headline naming the filter as the cause, and one button that relaxes that filter.
one_line_why: Show people what they're about to get, and always leave them a door out, a filter should be a promise, not a guess.

title: First-run onboarding: one question per screen, curated option lists
plain_english: When a new user answers questions during sign-up (interests, hair type, preferences), each screen should ask exactly one thing, so the progress bar actually means what it says. If a list of choices is long, show a curated handful first with a "show more" link, instead of dumping everything or hiding it all behind one vague button. And when a picker has a target number to reach, the button itself should say how many more are needed, like "Continue 3/3", so the user does not have to look elsewhere to check.
the_rule: One decision per onboarding screen. Show roughly 8 to 9 options before a numbered "Show more (N)" link. Use a continuous progress bar for active-choice screens, dot pagination plus a corner Skip only for passive value carousels. A multi-select picker with a target count folds that count into its own CTA label (e.g. "Continue 3/3"). Selected pills stay Solen's locked calm-gray fill, not the blue or black fill every sampled app uses, that mismatch is noted, not adopted.
tier_summary: CONV, cross-app convergence (Headway, Best Buy, X, Amazon Alexa, Tinder, Cosmos, live Fresha check), independently re-verified, not a controlled study
top_sources: Headway (Mobbin capture, iOS)
Best Buy interest picker (Mobbin capture)
Tinder + Cosmos counted-CTA pattern (Mobbin captures)
before_state: Not covered yet, Solen has no documented rule for how first-run onboarding screens should sequence questions, disclose long option lists, or signal progress.
after_state: A named default exists: one question per screen, an 8 to 9 item visible cap with a numbered show-more link, bar vs dot progress matched to screen type, and counted CTAs for target-count pickers, all while keeping Solen's own calm-gray selected-pill fill instead of copying the industry blue or black fill.
visual_demo_desc: Wrong: an interest-picker screen dumping 20+ pills at once with no grouping or disclosure, and a plain static "Continue" button with no count. Right: the same screen showing 8 to 9 pills under a section header, a "Mehr anzeigen (12)" link below, a thin progress bar at top, and the CTA reading "Continue 3/3" once 3 pills are selected, pills kept in Solen's calm-gray selected fill.
one_line_why: A progress bar only earns trust when every screen behind it asks exactly one question.

title: Match the notification's loudness to how urgent it actually is
plain_english: Not every notification deserves the same volume. A booking confirmation or a payment failure is urgent, so it should push to the phone with a sound and a badge. A "come back and rebook" nudge is not urgent, so it should only ever show up quietly inside the app (a toast or banner), never as a phone push. If low-value nudges get the loud treatment too, people mute the whole channel, including the messages they actually need to see.
the_rule: Three-rung ladder by message type: (1) urgent/transactional (booking confirmed, appointment reminder, payment failed) = phone push + sound + badge. (2) transactional but not urgent (document ready, review request) = phone push, no badge. (3) non-urgent/re-engagement (rebooking nudge, Inspo digest, promo) = in-app only (the existing Toast or a banner), never a phone push, never a badge. Inside the app: unread = a small dot plus bold title, never a colored full-row fill. Urgency shows as a status pill changing color (neutral to amber) plus a small yellow card, never a sudden red block. This rule only decides which surface a message uses, not how often it can fire, that stays the existing PSYCHOLOGY law 14 cap.
tier_summary: Apple's official notification guidelines (T1) and Android's official channel-importance docs (CONV, verified live) as the backbone, plus two peer-reviewed interruption-cost papers (T2) and direct re-checks of Fresha, GetYourGuide and Lyft's real screens (CONV)
top_sources: Apple Human Interface Guidelines (Notifications, Badging)
Android Developers (notification channels/importance docs)
Fresha app screens via Mobbin (confirmed-to-action-required pill pattern)
before_state: Solen has no rule that decides which surface (phone push, badge, or in-app toast) a given notification should use. Only the cadence cap exists (PSYCHOLOGY law 14, how many pushes per week), nothing about matching urgency to loudness.
after_state: A fixed three-step rule: urgent stuff gets a real phone push with sound and a badge, less-urgent transactional stuff gets a push without a badge, and anything promotional or re-engagement-only stays inside the app as a toast or banner and never becomes a phone push. Unread rows get a small dot and bold text, never a solid color fill. Urgency escalates through a pill color change, not a sudden loud red block.
visual_demo_desc: Wrong: a notification list row for an unread item painted with a full colored background fill, looking like an alert or error. Right: the same row on white with just a small dot next to the timestamp and the title in semibold, calm and scannable.
one_line_why: A push you didn't need to get is the reason you mute the push you actually needed.

title: Trust signals: labeled rows, not badge walls
plain_english: This is about anything meant to make a customer trust a salon or the platform: verified checkmarks, credential lines, review counts. Research (Stanford's credibility study, plus how Airbnb, Angi and others actually build this) shows trust reads best as a short, plain text row with a small checkmark, never a wall of badges or logos. Piling on trust badges backfires: it starts to look like the app is compensating for something.
the_rule: Max 1 credibility marker per type, 2-3 markers total per card, shown as a labeled row (small checkmark + short text), never a badge grid. Verification checkmarks are green or ink, never blue (blue is reserved for things you can tap). If there's nothing to show (e.g. zero reviews), omit the row entirely rather than showing a placeholder or a bare 0.
tier_summary: Stanford Guidelines for Web Credibility, Fogg 2002 (T2), corroborated by Fresha's live zero-review-row omission and Airbnb/Angi's labeled-row verification pattern (T3)
top_sources: Stanford Guidelines for Web Credibility (Fogg 2002)
NNGroup, Trustworthy Design (2016)
Fresha live search render (measured 2026-07-22)
before_state: Solen has no verification badge or trust-marker system yet (confirmed by grep, zero components implement one), and no written rule for how one should look or be colored if built. The one existing related piece, the salon card's rating row, already correctly hides itself when there are zero reviews rather than showing a placeholder, so that part is already right by accident, not by a documented rule.
after_state: A locked default recipe exists for the day Solen builds any trust marker: a short labeled row (checkmark + text), capped at one per type and 2-3 total per card, colored green or ink (never blue, since it is not tappable), and omitted entirely when there is no real data behind it. Nothing ships visually yet since Solen has no verification data to back a badge, but the shape and color rule is now written down so it is not invented ad hoc later.
visual_demo_desc: Wrong: a salon card with a stacked row of colorful badges/logos (blue verified shield, certification icons, a badge wall) crowding the card like Temu's checkout. Right: the same card with one quiet grey line, a small green checkmark plus "Verified" text, sitting under the salon name, no logos, no color noise.
one_line_why: A few credible signals build trust; a wall of badges reads as an app trying too hard to convince you.

title: Confirm rarely, name the exact error always
plain_english: Right now Solen has no clear rule for when to interrupt a user with a "are you sure?" popup versus just letting them undo something. This addition says: only pop up a confirmation for genuinely rare, costly, hard-to-reverse actions like cancelling a paid booking. For everyday reversible actions, like removing a discount code, just do it and give an undo link. It also says every error message must name the exact field and the exact reason, never a vague "something went wrong."
the_rule: Confirmation dialogs only for rare, destructive, hard-to-reverse actions (cancel a paid booking, delete a service with existing bookings); everyday reversible actions get an undo toast instead, never a confirm popup. Every error message must name the specific field and the specific cause the backend already knows (not a generic "invalid" message), and a failed form must never wipe out what the user typed.
tier_summary: Nielsen H5/H9 and WCAG 3.3.1-3.3.3 (T1/T2 academic floor), confirmed live on Fresha and Square's actual cancel-booking screens (CONV real-app evidence)
top_sources: Nielsen Norman Group (confirmation dialogs and error message guidelines)
Baymard Institute (adaptive validation error messages)
Fresha and Square Appointments live cancel-flow screens (Mobbin)
before_state: Solen has ErrorState and ErrorFallback components for showing errors, and a rule against silently swallowing errors in code, but no stated rule for when a destructive action needs a confirm popup versus an undo toast, and no rule that error messages must name the specific cause.
after_state: Confirm dialogs get reserved for a short list of truly costly, hard-to-reverse actions (paid-booking cancel, deleting a service with bookings), styled with Solen's existing ink CTA and full verb-phrase button labels ("Termin stornieren" / "Behalten"), never a bare Yes/No. Everything else reversible skips the popup and gets an undo toast. Every field error names the exact field and reason, and failed forms keep the user's typed input.
visual_demo_desc: Wrong: a generic confirm popup with bare "Yes / No" buttons on a routine action (like removing a discount code), plus a form field showing a vague red "Invalid" message that wiped the typed value. Right: the discount-code removal just happens with an inline "Rueckgaengig" undo link in a toast, and next to it a booking-cancel confirm uses ink "Termin stornieren" / "Behalten" buttons, with a field error below reading "Postleitzahl muss 4 Ziffern haben" and the typed value still in the box.
one_line_why: A confirm popup used on every action just trains people to click through it blind, so save it for the moments that actually matter, and always tell people exactly what went wrong.

title: Accessibility beyond color contrast
plain_english: Accessibility is not just "text is readable against the background." It also covers whether a customer can book using only a keyboard, whether a screen reader can announce what a button does, whether flashy animations respect a phone's "reduce motion" setting, and whether buttons are big enough to tap reliably. Some Solen customers will rely on exactly these things, and today a few of the pieces are either missing, duplicated and broken, or correctly built but not written down anywhere anyone would check.
the_rule: Two different tap-target numbers exist and must not be confused: 24x24 pixels is the legal minimum (WCAG 2.2, level AA), 44x44 pixels is the higher standard (WCAG level AAA, matching Apple's own guideline). Solen's buttons are already locked at 44px, which is the higher bar, not the bare minimum, but the design docs currently mislabel it as just "WCAG 2.1" without saying which level it meets.
tier_summary: Official W3C WCAG 2.2 standard (top-tier evidence), cross-checked live against Uber's own published accessibility statement
top_sources: W3C WCAG 2.2 official standard
Uber public accessibility statement (live-fetched)
Mobbin real-app scout (Discord, Canva, NYTimes)
before_state: Solen's design docs already state a 44px minimum tap-target size, but label it simply as "WCAG 2.1" without saying whether that is the legal floor or a higher bar (it is actually the higher one). The mobile menu is missing a "navigation" landmark that screen readers rely on to jump around the page. There are two competing "skip to content" links in the code: one that works correctly, and a second, unused one whose own code comment wrongly claims it's the one actually running. The "reduce motion" setting is correctly respected in the site's core styling, but that fact is not written into the accessibility checklist anyone would read before building a new animated feature.
after_state: The docs get corrected to name the legal minimum (24px) and the higher standard Solen already meets (44px) as two separate, clearly labeled things instead of one vague number. The missing navigation landmark on the mobile menu becomes a flagged, one-line fix, no visual change needed. The broken duplicate skip-link gets retired or its comment corrected so nobody trusts a link that isn't actually running. And the reduce-motion rule gets a pointer added to the checklist so the next person building an animation knows it already exists and not to rebuild it.
one_line_why: A rule that's correctly built but invisible in the checklist gets rebuilt wrong, or not found at all, the next time someone needs it.

title: Waiting screens: be instant when safe, be honest when not
plain_english: Some bookings can't fail (Solen just confirms itself), so those should jump straight to a green checkmark with no waiting screen at all. Others really do depend on someone else (a salon accepting, a payment finishing), and those need a loading skeleton plus one honest sentence with a real time estimate, like "usually confirmed within a few minutes." No app worth copying fakes a progress bar or a percentage to make a wait feel more important than it is, and Solen shouldn't either.
the_rule: Backend can't fail (self-confirming booking) = resolve instantly to the green checkmark, no interstitial. Backend depends on someone else (salon accepts, payment confirms) = show a shape-matched skeleton (shimmer sweep) plus one line with a real, specific time estimate ("meist innerhalb weniger Minuten"). Never a fake progress bar or invented percentage, and only add a route's loading skeleton if the fetch can plausibly take more than about 1 second.
tier_summary: Nielsen's 1993 response-time bands (T1) plus real confirmation-screen copy from Booking.com, Airbnb, OpenTable (T3, Mobbin captures, wording verified near word-for-word)
top_sources: Jakob Nielsen, Usability Engineering 1993 (response-time limits)
Buell and Norton 2011, Management Science (labor illusion / operational transparency)
Mobbin captures of Booking.com, Airbnb, OpenTable confirmation screens
before_state: Solen's RATIONALE.md has a short four-bullet "perceived performance" note that cites a wrong source (says Harrison 2010/CHI, actually 2007/UIST) and gives no concrete rule for when to show an instant result versus a waiting screen. Only 7 of 172 pages in the app currently have any loading skeleton at all, an unplanned gap, not a deliberate choice.
after_state: A clear, two-path rule replaces the vague note: self-contained bookings get an instant green check (already Solen's locked style), external-dependency bookings get a shimmer skeleton with one honest, real time estimate. The wrong citation is fixed, and there's now a stated default for when a route needs a loading skeleton (roughly, whenever a fetch could take more than a second).
visual_demo_desc: Wrong: a generic spinner or a fake animated progress bar with vague text like "Processing..." on a salon-confirmation screen. Right: two panels side by side, an instant green checkmark "Confirmed" for a self-accepting booking, and a shimmer-sweep skeleton with the honest line "Salon bestätigt meist innerhalb weniger Minuten" for a salon that manually confirms.
one_line_why: A wait that tells the truth about how long it'll actually take earns more trust than a fake progress bar ever could.

title: Copy mechanics: labels, errors, empty states
plain_english: This adds concrete size rules for four kinds of copy: button labels, error messages, reading level, and empty/confirmation screens. It does not change Solen's voice (the German du-form, no-hype tone stays locked), it only sets how long each piece of text should be and what it must contain so nothing reads like a wall of text or a vague dead end.
the_rule: Commit buttons (pay, book, confirm) get 1 to 4 words naming the thing, never a bare verb or a sentence. Error messages must say what happened, why in plain terms, what to do next, and never blame the user, and should name the exact field (not just "Required"). Copy should read at roughly grade 6 to 9 reading level (German/French/Italian judged by ear, not by an English formula). Empty and confirmation screens get exactly two lines: a 2 to 5 word headline plus one 8 to 15 word sub-line naming the next action, everything else below is label:value pairs, never prose, and the sub-line must never just repeat the headline (the Nike Run Club mistake).
tier_summary: NN/g error-message guidelines and Nielsen's recognition-over-recall heuristic (T2), corroborated by direct, re-verified screen captures on Square Go and Nike Run Club
top_sources: Nielsen Norman Group (Error-Message Guidelines, Plain Language Experts)
Mobbin screen captures (Square Go, Nike Run Club, Fresha, IKEA)
Flesch/Kincaid readability research
before_state: Solen has a copy-economy rule (drop redundant words, truncate long text with "Mehr lesen") but no sourced floor for button-label length, no required error-message structure, no reading-level target, and no fixed two-line pattern for empty or confirmation screens.
after_state: Every commit button, error string, and empty/confirmation screen gets checked against a concrete word-count and structure floor before shipping, catching vague errors like a bare "Required" and headline-repeats-itself empty states like Nike Run Club's.
visual_demo_desc: Wrong: an empty "no bookings" screen where the headline "No Appointments" is followed by a sub-line that just restates it ("You have no appointments"), plus a vague error "Required" under a blank field. Right: same screen with headline "No Appointments" and sub-line "Explore nearby salons and find your new go-to today", plus error "Please enter your phone number so we can confirm your booking."
one_line_why: A sub-line that just repeats its own headline is a wasted sentence, and a bare "Required" is a locked door with no handle.

title: Web stays light-only, on purpose (dark mode is a mobile-only feature)
plain_english: Solen's website will never get a dark mode toggle, and this addition writes down exactly why, so it reads as a deliberate choice instead of a gap nobody explained. The short version: reading performance research shows light mode is at least as good as dark mode for text, and every direct competitor checked (Fresha, Vagaro, Doctolib) also skips dark mode on their website. Dark mode stays a mobile-app-only feature, since that is the one place the owner actually uses it daily.
the_rule: Web ships light-only, no dark mode toggle at all, full stop. Backing: 0 of 9 checked competitor/marketplace websites (Fresha, Vagaro, Doctolib verified live, plus 6 more observed) offer a dark mode toggle. Mobile keeps its own separate dark theme (already built, THEMING.md), this rule only covers the website.
tier_summary: Piepenbrock et al. 2013/2014 reading research (T1) plus corrected Nielsen Norman Group findings (T2) plus live competitor check on Fresha, Vagaro, Doctolib (T2)
top_sources: Piepenbrock, Mayr, Mund and Buchner (2013/2014 reading studies)
Nielsen Norman Group, dark-mode article (re-verified, corrected)
Fresha.com, Vagaro.com, Doctolib.fr (checked live)
before_state: Web already has no dark mode, but the reasoning was thin and partly wrong: an earlier draft claimed Nielsen Norman Group says "commit to dark mode fully or don't bother," which is not what that source actually says.
after_state: The light-only decision is now written down correctly with real sourcing: Nielsen Norman Group actually recommends offering an optional dark toggle, but Solen is deliberately choosing not to (for cost and to match how every competitor's website behaves), and that tradeoff is now stated honestly instead of hidden behind a made-up quote.
one_line_why: Staying light on web isn't Solen falling behind, it's Solen matching every other booking site in its category, on purpose.

title: Loading and wait states: skeleton, scrim, or full block
plain_english: This adds a clear decision tree for what the screen should show while something loads, on top of the timing numbers Solen already has. Short waits get a skeleton shaped like the real content, medium waits dim the existing screen in place instead of blanking it, and only a genuinely long, uncancelable wait (like a payment) earns a full-screen block, and only with a message telling the user how long to expect. This matters for a booking app because payment, availability checks, and confirmation are exactly the moments users get anxious about, and the wrong loading treatment (a blank screen, a moved button, a bare spinner) reads as broken even when it isn't.
the_rule: Wait under 1 second: show a skeleton shaped to the final content, never a bare spinner. Wait roughly 1-3 seconds tied to one action: dim the existing content in place (a scrim), keep the CTA visible but disabled, never hide or move it. Only a long, uncancelable operation (payment, booking confirmation) gets a full-screen blocking state, and it must carry explicit time-expectation copy such as "may take up to a minute, please don't close". Success confirmation stays a pastel inline banner or pill (tint background, ink text, saturated icon), never a full-bleed celebratory takeover. Separately, Solen's locked "snap" easing curve, cubic-bezier(0.4,0,0.2,1), is confirmed live in production by two real booking competitors (Booksy exact match, Treatwell close cousin), not just a spec-page value.
tier_summary:
web.dev RAIL and INP (T2, re-confirmed by direct fetch) plus live-measured production CSS from Booksy and Treatwell (CONV); wait-state pattern itself is lower-confidence (T3, from a Mobbin app survey, flagged for spot-check after a sibling claim about Vagaro failed re-verification)</tier_summary>

after_state: RATIONALE.md gets a new subsection with the wait-state decision tree above, plus the easing curve claim upgraded from "looks Material-like" to "confirmed live in two real competitors' production code."
