Right: the time-slot list stays visible but dimmed, the Buchen button stays in place just disabled, and only if the wait is a real payment step does the screen fully block, with a line of copy saying roughly how long it will take.
one_line_why: The shape of the wait matters as much as its length: show the user what's coming, never a blank screen where the button used to be.

title: Shadows and pop-up layers, checked against real apps
plain_english: This checks two things Solen already locked: how a shadow gets stronger as something lifts higher (like a modal popping above the page), and how pop-up layers (sheets, modals, toasts) get stacked so they never fight each other. Real competitor apps, Fresha, Booking.com, Booksy, and Treatwell, were measured live and they do the same thing Solen already does: a shadow gets both blurrier and darker together as it lifts, and layer numbers jump in big rounded steps with one huge reserved number kept for things that must always sit on top, like a cookie banner.
the_rule: Keep Solen's shadow recipe as is: blur 3px, 12px, 28px and darkness .04, .08, .12 across the three lift levels, both growing together, never just one alone. Keep the current pop-up layer numbers (400/410/500/510/600/700) unchanged for now. Flag, but do not act on, a real mismatch: competitors use big round jumps (1, 10, 100, 1000, 2000) plus one giant reserved number near 2,147,483,647 for must-always-win overlays, instead of Solen's tighter, evenly-spaced steps.
tier_summary: Physical optics (T1) plus live-measured competitor CSS on Fresha, Booking.com, Booksy and Treatwell (T1), backed by Material Design's named shadow system (convention-tier)
top_sources: Fresha (live-measured CSS)
Booking.com and Booksy (live-measured CSS)
Bootstrap 5.3 z-index docs
before_state: Solen already has a locked shadow recipe (three strength levels) and a locked set of pop-up layer numbers (400 to 700), but neither had been checked against what real competitor apps actually ship.
after_state: Same numbers, same rules, nothing changes today. What's new is proof: real competitor apps grow shadows the same way Solen does, and a clearly flagged (not yet acted on) gap between Solen's tight layer-number steps and the wide, round-jump steps every measured competitor actually uses.
visual_demo_desc: Wrong: three lifted cards where only the blur increases (same faint darkness at every level, top card looks pasted-on and washed out). Right: three lifted cards where blur AND darkness both climb together (3px/.04 resting, 12px/.08 raised, 28px/.12 top), so the top card visibly reads as furthest off the page.
one_line_why: A shadow that only gets bigger without getting darker never convinces the eye the object actually lifted.

title: Why Solen's four colors work together (and why blue text breaks on gray)
plain_english: Solen's four locked colors (near-black text, blue links, and two grays) were picked by eye over several rounds, but nobody had proven they actually form one coherent color family. Running them through proper color math shows they do: the two grays share almost the exact same undertone, and the old warm grays we replaced were simply that same family rotated to a different hue, not a random redo. It also proves, with real numbers, why blue link text passes contrast on a white background but fails on the gray sunken background, so anyone adding a new gray or checking contrast later has a formula to check against instead of eyeballing it.
the_rule: Blue accent text (#276EF1) passes accessibility contrast on white (4.58:1) but fails on the gray sunken background (4.17:1, below the 4.5:1 minimum). Rule: never place blue accent text on the sunken gray surface, only on white or near-white. Also: drop the "accent contrast is about 3.7:1" figure some brief cited, it does not exist anywhere in Solen's docs and must never be repeated.
tier_summary: Ottosson OKLCH color math + WCAG contrast formula (both T1, textbook-standard), corroborated more loosely by live-measured competitor sites (Fresha, Booksy, Booking.com) at CONV/T3 level
top_sources: Bjorn Ottosson, "A perceptual color space for image processing" (2020)
W3C WCAG 2.1 Success Criterion 1.4.3 contrast formula
Live getComputedStyle measurement of Fresha.com, Booksy.com, Booking.com
before_state: The four locked hexes (ink, accent blue, border gray, sunken gray) existed as owner-approved literals in LOCKFILE with no documented proof they form one coherent family, and a stray "accent contrast is about 3.7:1" figure was floating around unsourced.
after_state: The two grays are shown to share the same undertone within a fraction of a degree, the old warm grays are shown to be the same family just rotated to a different hue, the blue accent's contrast failure on gray is traced to its exact color-math position, and the wrong 3.7:1 number is retired for good. No hex values change, this only documents and proves what was already locked.
one_line_why: Good color systems are provable, not just approved: the math should explain why a rule exists, not just declare it.

title: Translated text needs room by string length, not by language
plain_english: When German, French, or Italian text is longer than the English original, the amount of extra room it needs depends on how SHORT the original word was, not on which language it's translated into. Short labels like button text and tab chips need the most room (they can nearly triple in length), while long sentences need the least. When a translated word still doesn't fit, real apps fix it by shortening the wording, widening the button or chip, or wrapping to a second line, never by shrinking the font or cutting the word off mid-way.
the_rule: Size fixed-width slots (chips, tabs, buttons) by source character count: under 10 characters plan for +100-200% length, 11-20 chars +80-100%, 21-30 chars +60-80%, 31-50 chars +40-60%, 51-70 chars +40-70% (the source data has a known bump here), over 70 chars +30%. Test with an Italian and French string too, not just German (Italian ran 3.0x vs German 2.8x vs French 2.6x on one real example). If a string still overflows: shorten the copy first, widen the container second, wrap to a second line third. Never shrink the font or truncate mid-word on a CTA or chip.
tier_summary: W3C/IBM published expansion table (T2) plus live 2026-07-22 checks of Fresha, Treatwell, Booksy, Doctolib, N26 showing real apps shorten, widen, or wrap instead of truncating
top_sources: W3C Internationalization: Text size in translation (Richard Ishida, citing IBM)
Live fetches of Fresha, Treatwell, Booksy, Doctolib (2026-07-22)
